title: Ang 347–348: Asa begins
hookLine: So Dar again, now as the raga's first hymn
tomorrow: what should you ask about someone new first?

cards: A favorite song comes on in a different version: slower, a new key, a live recording with the crowd singing. Same words, and it lands somewhere new.
On ang 347, Raag Asa opens with a hymn you may have met twice already on this walk: So Dar, what is that door? It's in the Japji. It's in the evening Rehras.
And here it is again, at the head of Asa, with the raga written above it. So why sing it again, and how?

teach.b: So Dar asks, in paraphrase: what is that door, what is that house, where You sit and care for all? The answer is a crowd of singers. Wind, water and fire sing.

teach.h: ALL OF CREATION SINGS AT IT.
teach.b: Countless instruments play. And the hymn itself counts the music: so many ragas, so many singers. Here it stands at the door of a raga, set to be sung in Asa.
That opens a real conversation among Sikhs about kirtan, and both sides deserve their best case.

teach.h: SING IT IN THE NAMED RAGA.
teach.b: One view: sing it in the raga the heading names. The Gurus placed each hymn under a raga on purpose; the raga carries a mood, and the mood is part of what the hymn teaches. Learn it, even if it's slow to learn.

teach.h: A TUNE THE WHOLE ROOM CAN SING.
teach.b: The other view: the Word is what matters most, and a simple, familiar tune lets a whole room, kids included, sing along and understand.
A melody nobody can follow keeps people outside the door. Both sides love this hymn and want it in people's mouths.
They differ on what gets you through the door first: the sound the Gurus named, or a sound the room already knows. The hymn just keeps listing singers.

how: In gurdwaras, kirtan of Gurbani is sung by ragis, sometimes in the raga named in the Granth's heading and sometimes in simpler, familiar tunes; So Dar is also part of the evening Rehras that Sikhs say daily.

the page where Raag Asa begins with So Dar
the page holding the Sohila at night

games.q: the door again — tap the pairs.
p: the mood is part of the teaching

s: So Dar appears only once in the Guru Granth Sahib
it's in the Japji, in the evening Rehras, and again at the head of Asa on ang 347.
So Dar itself names ragas and singers at the door
the hymn counts so many ragas, so many singers, with wind, water and fire among them.
Sikhs all agree kirtan must be sung in the named raga
it's a live conversation: some favor the named raga, some favor familiar tunes.

games.q: your cousin wants the wedding kirtan in a tune the guests already know. you agree with her. what's the strongest case for the raga instead?
o: the Gurus set each hymn in a raga; its mood is part of what it teaches.
ragas are older, and older ways are always more correct.
a tune people already know makes the words harder to hear.
games.why: that's the raga side at its best. the other side's best: a tune the room knows lets everyone sing the Word together. both want the hymn sung.

practice: If you can, play a recording of So Dar sung in Raag Asa, or read ang 347 slowly to yourself. Then let the room's own sounds take over: the hum of a fridge, a car outside, your breath.
The hymn hears wind and water singing at that door; for the sit, just listen.
